comments.author: @leechumbley5440
comments.text: Again I am humbled by how much I have learned in this video. I knew nothing about the Enlarged Homestead Act, the immigration and then the mass exodus when the wheat harvests failed and the cattle died – reminniscent of the 1930s Dust Bowl in Oklahoma. How interesting that the capital of Helena was a quickly thrown up settlement after the Last Chance Gulch struck gold.  I knew absolutely nothing about the copper boom in Butte, much like the silver boom once in Potosí in Bolivia. I once saw an article with a photo of a huge hole in the earth and frightful mention of poisoned water, but only knew it was “somewhere in Montana“ without any context. With the Westinghouse-Edison electicity ‘wars’ the whole world economy went crazy for electricity and the indispensible copper wiring that entailed. The story of the near extermination of the bison as cruel sadistic policy turns any sensible person’s stomach. The Buffalo Treaty is a positive and welcome thing. Thank you.

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That Potosí comparison is a sharp one - copper in Butte and silver in Potosí both left behind that same haunting legacy of a boomtown built on extraction, then a landscape scarred long after the money moved on. The Berkeley Pit is likely the hole you saw in that article; its poisoned water is exactly the kind of long-tail cost that doesn't make headlines until decades later. And you're right that the bison policy was deliberate and brutal, which makes the Buffalo Treaty's modern restoration effort feel like real, hard-won progress. Thank you for such a thorough, engaged read.

comments.author: @TravelHorizon-4K
comments.text: It’s a striking contradiction how Bison are celebrated and restored by Native nations in the North, yet slaughtered at Yellowstone's southern border to protect the cattle industry from potential disease. Are economic interests in ranching being prioritized too heavily over true ecological restoration?
